newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss vote to keep arms sales, maintain EU talks.
newsitem.headline: Swiss vote to keep arms sales, maintain EU talks.

text.p: Swiss voters on Sunday rejected a bid by left-wing parties to ban the country's lucrative arms trade but they also turned down a move by hard-right groups that could have killed any accord with the European Union.

A massive 77.3 per cent vote to keep arms exports, which brought in 233 million Swiss francs ($166 million) last year, came as a relief to weapons manufacturers as well as the coalition government which had opposed the measure.

Sunday's referendum on the issue was held in the shadow of recent revelations that the vast bulk of Switzerland's foreign arms sales during World War Two had gone to the Axis powers, Nazi Germany and Fascist Italy.

Proponents of a ban, including the Socialist Party which holds two seats in the seven-member coalition cabinet, argued it was hypocrisy to provide development aid to poor countries at the same time as selling them weapons.
"Arms deliveries reduce the chances for political and non-violent conflict resolution and fuel regional arms races," the coordinating committee of the groups which forced the referendum argued.

But amid concern over climbing unemployment and a troubled economy, the call found little response -- especially among traditional-minded voters in German-speaking Switzerland who are increasingly angered over attacks on the country's wartime role.

In most German-speaking cantons, well over 80 per cent of the voters turning out opposed a ban, with 89.9 per cent saying "no" in the Nidwald canton where Switzerland's Pilatus propeller-driven trainer aircraft is produced.

The Pilatus, which in the past has been at the centre of controversy when some purchasing states fitted it with weaponry and used it for anti-insurgency operations, would have fallen under the ban as a potentially dual-purpose product.

Opponents of a ban had argued that job losses in the pure arms industry could have totalled nearly 6,000 if the vote -- for which only 35 per cent of the electorate turned out -- had gone the other way.
But they said a ban could also have affected some 122,000 jobs in industries like electronics and mechanical engineering which produce other "dual purpose" items including computer components.

Support for the veto was relatively strong in French-speaking western Switzerland, in a new confirmation of differing views on global issues and the country's role in the world between the two main linguistic communities.

In Geneva canton, which includes the international city, 39 per cent of the voters backed a ban, while 28 per cent supported it in the neighbouring Vaud canton and 27 per cent in Neuchatel in the north-west.

But both main communities came out equally strongly with an average of 73.9 per cent rejecting a right-wing measure that would have forced the government to seek advance referendum approval of any proposal in its long-running EU negotiations.
The measure was clearly designed by fiercely nationalistic groups in German- and Italian-speaking Switzerland to make impossible any economic and transport agreement with Brussels.

Opinion polls suggest that the majority of all Swiss people -- who in 1992 rejected ties through the European Economic Area linking the EU to the European Free Trade Association (EFTA) -- would still oppose EU membership.

But most appear to recognise that the loose overall agreement on trade and commercial ties that the Berne coalition government hopes to conclude within the next few weeks is needed and would not infringe on the country's sovereignty.
